diffusion-types-s2.title: Sequoyah and the Cherokee syllabary
diffusion-types-s2.html:
Sequoyah and the Cherokee syllabary (LevlPrep summary, 2026)

Sequoyah, a Cherokee silversmith born about 1770, could not read English, but he watched English speakers send messages on paper. He became convinced that the Cherokee language could be written too. By 1821 he had finished a syllabary: a set of 86 symbols, each standing for a syllable of spoken Cherokee rather than a single sound. Some symbols look like Latin letters, but they stand for completely different sounds. Within a few years many Cherokee people could read and write, and in 1828 the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper began printing in Cherokee and English.

agricultural-origins-s2.title: The potato in Ireland
agricultural-origins-s2.html: LevlPrep summary, 2026, based on historians' accounts. The potato was domesticated in the Andes of South America. Spanish ships carried it to Europe in the late 1500s, and it reached Ireland soon after. The potato grew well in Ireland's cool, wet climate and fed a family on a small plot. By the 1840s, millions of poor rural families in Ireland depended on one kind of potato for most of their food. From 1845, a plant disease called blight destroyed the crop several years in a row. In the famine that followed, about 1 million people died and more than 1 million left Ireland, many for the United States.

items.q: People in Europe long called Southwest Asia and North Africa "the Middle East". What kind of direction does that name use?
options: Relative direction: "east" only from the point of view of Europe
Absolute direction: the region is east of the whole world
Absolute direction: it measures east from the North Pole
Relative distance: it measures how long the trip from Europe took
Absolute location: the latitude and longitude of the region

why.correct: Relative directions such as "the Far East" or "out West" change with the speaker's location.
options: Right: relative direction depends on where the speaker stands. From India, the same region lies to the west.
Absolute directions are compass directions that do not depend on a viewpoint, and nothing is east of the whole world.
Compass directions are not measured from the North Pole in this way.
The name is about direction, not travel time.
Absolute location is a position on the grid; "Middle East" names a direction seen from Europe.

items.q: What do the lines on this map join?
options: Places with the same number of people per square kilometer
Points that are the same distance from the South Coast
The borders between the provinces of Country A
Points that are the same height above sea level
Roads that climb from the South Coast up to the uplands

why.correct: An isoline joins places with the same value. On this map the value is height above sea level, so the lines show elevation.
options: Lines of equal population density would need population data; this map's values are heights in meters.
The lines are labeled in meters above sea level, not distance.
Province borders are the thin gray lines; the labeled lines cross them.
Right: an isoline joins points of equal value; the legend says the value here is height in meters.
A reference map would show roads; these lines carry values of height.

items.q: Where is the land steepest, and how can you tell?
options: Near the South Coast, where the lowest line is drawn
Along the South Coast, where the 100 meter line meets the sea
In the east, where the lines are farthest apart
In the middle of the country, where the 500 meter line runs north to south
In the Western Uplands, where the lines are closest together

why.correct: The spacing of isolines shows slope: close together is steep, far apart is gentle.
options: The coast is the lowest land, and the lines near it are far apart, so it is gentle.
The coast is the lowest, flattest land; steep land shows where the lines crowd together.
Lines far apart mean the height changes slowly: gentle land.
The 500 meter line is in the middle, but the lines around it are widely spaced.
Right: close lines mean the height changes a lot over a short distance, which is a steep slope.

items.q: A company in Country A wants flat, low land for a large new port and warehouses. Using the map, which area fits best?
options: The South Coast, below 100 meters, where the lines are far apart
The Western Uplands, above 1,500 meters
The east, above 1,000 meters, where the lines are far apart
The middle of the country, between the 500 and 1,000 meter lines
The north of the Western Uplands, where the lines bunch together

why.correct: Read both the values (low) and the spacing (gentle) to choose flat, low land.
options: Right: the land there is low and the wide spacing shows it is gentle.
That is the highest land and, with close lines, the steepest.
Land above 1,000 meters lies in the west, by the Western Uplands; a port needs low, flat land on the coast.
That land is higher and still well inland from the coast.
Bunched lines mean steep slopes, the opposite of what the company needs.

items.q: Brazil's space research agency uses satellite images to track how much of the Amazon rainforest is cleared each year. Why is remote sensing a good fit for this job?
options: It measures a huge, remote forest the same way every year
It replaces maps, so planners can stop using them
It records why each farmer decided to clear part of the forest
It needs no computers or experts, so it is cheap and quick to run
It shows the forest at the local scale and no other

why.correct: Remote sensing suits large areas and repeated measurement; it cannot record people's reasons.
options: Right: satellites cover vast areas regularly, so changes from year to year can be compared.
Satellite images are often turned into maps; remote sensing fits because it measures a huge, remote forest the same way each year.
Reasons come from interviews or documents; images show what changed, not why.
Satellite images are processed by computers.
Images can be studied at many scales, from one hillside to the whole Amazon.

items.q: A student writes that this map shows data at the national scale, because it covers all of Country A. Which scale of analysis do the data show?
options: National, because the map covers the whole of one country
Global, because internet access is spreading around the world
Regional, because the provinces are grouped into four classes
Local (subnational), because each value is for one province
A large map scale, because the map shows one country in detail

why.correct: The scale of analysis is the scale of the data, not the size of the area drawn. Each shaded value is for one province, so the data are at the local (subnational) scale.
options: This is the slip the student made: a national value would be one number for all of Country A, and this map has eight.
A worldwide trend is not on this map; its values are for provinces of one country.
The four classes group values for the legend; they do not change what each value describes, which is one province.
Right: one value per province is local (subnational) data, even though the map covers the whole country.
Map scale is how much the map is reduced; the question asks about the scale of analysis, the level of the data.

items.q: Brazil built a new capital, Brasília, far inland in 1960 so that more people would live away from the coast. Which kind of factor shaping population distribution does this show?
options: A physical factor: the inland plateau had more ports
A physical factor: a better climate inland
A physical factor: new rivers inland
A human factor: a government decision
Environmental determinism: the land forced people to move

why.correct: Governments shape where people live. Brasília is a human factor at the national scale: a political decision drew people and jobs inland.
options: An inland plateau has no seaports; the move came from a government choice, a human factor.
the move was a government plan, not a change in climate.
no new rivers formed; the government chose the site.
Right: building a capital is a choice people make, so it is a human factor.
determinism says nature decides; here people decided.

items.q: Egypt has a moderate arithmetic density but a very high physiological density. What explains the difference?
options: Egypt counts its desert as farmland in its arable totals
Most Egyptians work as farmers
Very little of Egypt’s land can grow crops, and most of it is by the Nile
Egypt has more land that can grow crops than most countries in Africa and Asia
Egypt’s population is spread evenly over its desert

why.correct: Arithmetic density spreads Egypt’s people over all its land, including empty desert. Physiological density counts only arable land, which is about 3 percent of Egypt (World Bank, 2021 data), so its value is far higher.
options: Arable land is land that can grow crops; the desert is left out, which is why the farmland figure is small.
that would raise agricultural density; the gap here comes from how little land is arable.
Right: most of Egypt is desert, so a small area of farmland feeds a large population.
it is the reverse: Egypt has very little arable land.
Egypt’s people are clustered along the Nile.

items.q: Invented Country H has 40 million people, 400,000 square kilometers of land and 20,000 square kilometers of arable land. What is its physiological density?
options: 2,000 people per square kilometer of arable land
100 people per square kilometer of total land
200 people per square kilometer of arable land
A carrying capacity of 2,000 people
20,000 people per square kilometer of arable land

why.correct: Physiological density is people per unit of arable land: 40,000,000 / 20,000 = 2,000 people per square kilometer of farmland.
options: Right: 40,000,000 people / 20,000 square kilometers of arable land = 2,000.
100 per square kilometer uses all the land (40,000,000 / 400,000): that is arithmetic density.
Carrying capacity is how many people the land can support; physiological density is a measure of pressure, people per unit of farmland.
20,000 is the arable area itself, not people per square kilometer.

items.q: About what share of Country V's population is under age 15?
options: About 21%
About 15%
About 41%
About 56%
About 4%

why.correct: Add the three youngest groups on both sides: males 7.6 + 6.9 + 6.1 = 20.6 and females 7.3 + 6.7 + 6.0 = 20.0, so about 40.6%, or about 41%.
options: About 21% is one side only, the males (20.6); the share of the population counts both sides.
About 15% is the 0 to 4 group alone (7.6 + 7.3); ages 5 to 14 are under 15 too.
Right: the six bars for ages 0 to 14 add to about 41% of the population.
About 56% is ages 15 to 64, the working-age group.
About 4% is ages 65 and over, the top of the pyramid.

items.q: Which country’s rates are consistent with stage 3 of the demographic transition model?
options: Country R and Country T equally
Country S
Country R
Country T
Country U

why.correct: In stage 3 the death rate is already low and the birth rate is falling, so growth slows. Country S fits: 23 births and 6 deaths per 1,000.
options: R, with high births and low deaths, fits stage 2; T, with low and close rates, fits stage 4. Stage 3 is falling births with low deaths, as in S.
Right: its death rate is low (6) and its birth rate has fallen to 23, still well above deaths.
R’s birth rate is still very high (44): that fits stage 2.
T’s rates are both low and close: that fits stage 4.
U has more deaths than births: that fits stage 5.

items.q: A student writes, "Country U is in stage 1, because its population is barely changing." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Stage 1 countries have more births than deaths, so they grow fast
Stage 1 is defined by migration, not by births and deaths
Stage 1 has high rates; U has low birth and death rates
Country U is growing fast, so its data fit stage 2
No country can have more deaths than births in a year

why.correct: Slow or negative growth can come from high rates (stage 1) or low rates (stage 4 or 5). U’s rates are low, with deaths above births: consistent with stage 5. Readers in 2024 saw many answers place such countries in stage 1 or 2.
options: stage 1 rates are both high and close, so growth is slow there too.
The model's stages are set by birth and death rates; migration is not part of it.
Right: both stage 1 and stage 5 can show little growth, but for opposite reasons.
U has more deaths than births, so it is shrinking.
U does, and some real countries do too, such as Japan.

items.q: Country T’s leading causes of death are heart disease, cancer and stroke. Which stage of the epidemiological transition does this fit best?
options: Pestilence and famine
Receding pandemics
Reemergence of infectious and parasitic diseases
Degenerative and human-created diseases
Infections and illness in young children

why.correct: The epidemiological transition says the main causes of death shift from infections and famine toward chronic diseases such as heart disease and cancer. T fits the degenerative stage.
options: that stage is ruled by infections and hunger, with very high death rates.
in that stage infections are falling but still lead the causes of death.
In that stage infections come back as leading killers; Country T’s leading causes are heart disease, cancer and stroke.
Right: heart disease, cancer and stroke are chronic diseases of long lives and modern habits.
that is the pattern in Country R, not a stage name for T.

items.q: The first step of Path 1, from a village in Oaxaca to Mexico City, is which kind of move?
options: Chain migration to join relatives in the city
Transnational migration
Transhumance
Internal, rural-to-urban migration
Forced migration across an international border

why.correct: Internal migration is a move within one country. A move from a village to a big city is rural-to-urban migration, the largest kind of migration in many countries.
options: Chain migration is Path 2, where a brother and cousins follow the first migrant; this first step of Path 1 is a move from a village to a city inside Mexico.
that step does not cross a border.
transhumance is the seasonal moving of herds.
Right: it stays inside Mexico and goes from the countryside to a city.
the step stays inside Mexico, and nothing shows force.

items.q: What is one limitation of this map for explaining why the migrants moved?
options: It does not show where the migrants started their journeys
It leaves out the years in which the Path 2 migrants moved
It shows the moves at the global scale, so the countries are unclear
It is a real record of the many migrants from Oaxaca and Puebla
It shows routes and order, not causes

why.correct: Flow maps show direction, route and sometimes volume. They cannot show causes such as wages, drought or family ties: you need other sources for those.
options: the start of each path is marked on the map.
The map gives the years for Path 2 (1995, 2001, 2008). What it cannot show is why anyone moved.
the map shows two named countries and named cities.
the flows are invented for practice and show one family each.
Right: arrows show paths, not push or pull factors.

items.q: A baby born to parents from Japan is adopted by a family in São Paulo, Brazil, and raised there. As an adult, she speaks Portuguese, cheers for a Brazilian soccer club and cooks Brazilian food. What does her story show about culture?
options: Culture is set at birth by a person's family background
Culture is learned from the people around you, not inherited
Culture depends mostly on the climate of a person's birthplace
Culture spreads to a person through the food she eats as a baby
Culture is the same in Japan and in Brazil

why.correct: culture is passed on by teaching and living in a group. She learned the culture she grew up in, whatever her parents' origin.
options: Her story shows the opposite: she took on the culture of the place where she was raised.
Right: culture is passed on by teaching and living in a group. She learned the culture she grew up in, whatever her parents' origin.
She was raised in São Paulo and learned its culture. Where she was born did not decide it.
Food is one trait among many; her story shows that she learned language, sport and food from the people who raised her.
Japanese and Brazilian cultures differ in language, food and much more. Her story is about how culture is learned.

items.q: For many years, many restaurants in Saudi Arabia had separate sections and entrances for families and for single men. In 2019 the government said separate entrances were no longer required. What does this example show about the cultural landscape?
options: Ideas about gender shape how buildings divide space
The desert climate decides how restaurants are designed
Postmodern architecture usually calls for separate entrances
Separate entrances are a folk tradition found in each country
Restaurant layouts are part of the physical landscape

why.correct: the separate entrances were a mark of attitudes about how men and women share space. When rules changed, the built landscape could change too.
options: Right: the separate entrances were a mark of attitudes about how men and women share space. When rules changed, the built landscape could change too.
The rule was about who sits where, not about heat or dry air. Culture, not climate, drove the design.
Separate entrances follow social rules, not an architectural style.
The example is one country's rules about gender and space, and the 2019 change shows the rules were cultural and could change.
Anything people build is part of the cultural landscape, not the physical one.

items.q: Tanzania has more than 100 ethnic groups, most with their own language. After independence, its leaders promoted Swahili as a shared language in schools and government. Which statement best explains the result?
options: Tanzania's many languages became one creole by the 1970s
A shared language helped unite many groups as one country
Swahili split the country into separate language regions
Each ethnic group soon stopped using its home language
The policy is an example of the physical landscape at work

why.correct: when people from many groups can speak to each other in one language, they can share schools, news and politics. That makes the language a centripetal force.
options: Swahili was promoted alongside home languages; the many languages did not merge into one creole.
Right: when people from many groups can speak to each other in one language, they can share schools, news and politics. That makes the language a centripetal force.
Swahili was promoted everywhere, so it linked regions instead of splitting them.
Many Tanzanians speak Swahili beside their home language; promoting one shared language did not end the others.
Language policy is a human choice, part of culture and politics.

items.q: In a farming valley in Kenya, one farmer starts growing a new kind of bean and earns more. Her neighbors copy her the next year, then their neighbors the year after. Which kind of diffusion is this?
options: Relocation diffusion, because farmers move to new land
Contagious diffusion, spreading to nearby farms
Stimulus diffusion, because neighbors change the bean into rice
Hierarchical diffusion, starting with the largest farms
Stimulus diffusion, because neighbors invent a new crop

why.correct: the new bean spreads from farm to neighboring farm, like a ripple, which is contagious diffusion.
options: No one moved; neighbors copied the crop where they already lived.
Right: the new bean spreads from farm to neighboring farm, like a ripple, which is contagious diffusion.
The neighbors grow the same bean; stimulus diffusion would mean the idea is changed into something new.
The spread goes to the nearest farms, not from the biggest or most powerful first.
The neighbors plant the same bean, so the trait is not being changed into a new form.

items.q: Which kind of diffusion does Sequoyah's syllabary show?
options: Stimulus diffusion: the idea of writing spread and was reworked
Relocation diffusion: English speakers moved and brought writing
Reverse hierarchical diffusion from small towns up to large cities
Hierarchical diffusion: writing went from big cities to small towns
Contagious diffusion: Cherokee readers copied English words

why.correct: Sequoyah did not adopt English writing. He took the idea that speech can be written and built a new system for Cherokee.
options: Right: Sequoyah did not adopt English writing. He took the idea that speech can be written and built a new system for Cherokee.
English speakers did not bring the syllabary; Sequoyah created it. What spread was an idea, which he changed.
The passage gives no order of places by size; the idea of writing spread from English speakers to Sequoyah and was reworked on the way.
The passage says nothing about city size. The key point is that the idea was changed into a new form.
The syllabary writes Cherokee, not English words, and its symbols stand for different sounds.

items.q: Which detail from the passage best shows that the trait changed as it spread?
options: Sequoyah was a silversmith born in about 1770
Letter-like symbols stand for new sounds
The Cherokee Phoenix began printing in 1828
Many Cherokee people learned to read within a few years
Sequoyah watched English speakers send messages

why.correct: the shapes came from contact with English writing, but their meaning was new. A trait that spreads and changes is the mark of stimulus diffusion.
options: His job and birth year do not show anything about the trait changing.
Right: the shapes came from contact with English writing, but their meaning was new. A trait that spreads and changes is the mark of stimulus diffusion.
The newspaper shows that the syllabary was used, not that the idea of writing changed.
Fast learning shows how quickly it spread, not that the trait changed as it spread.
This shows how he met the idea, not how he changed it.

items.q: After 1821, many Cherokee people learned the syllabary from relatives and neighbors who already knew it. Which kind of diffusion describes this spread among the Cherokee?
options: Stimulus diffusion, because each reader made a new syllabary
Relocation diffusion, because readers moved to one town
Contagious diffusion, from person to person nearby
Hierarchical diffusion, from leaders down to everyone else
Reverse hierarchical diffusion, from small villages up to cities

why.correct: once it existed, the syllabary spread through direct contact between people close to each other, which is contagious diffusion.
options: Readers learned the same 86 symbols; they did not change them. Stimulus diffusion fits the first step, not this one.
The passage gives no move. People learned from those around them.
Right: once it existed, the syllabary spread through direct contact between people close to each other, which is contagious diffusion.
The question says people learned from relatives and neighbors, not from a top-down ladder.
The passage describes learning from relatives and neighbors, person to person, with no order of places by size.

items.q: Tok Pisin began in the 1800s as a simple trade and work language in what is now Papua New Guinea. Many children there now grow up speaking it as their first language, and it is an official language. What process does this show?
options: Creolization: a contact language gains native speakers
Ethnocentrism: one language is judged better than another
Relocation diffusion: speakers moved to Papua New Guinea
Hierarchical diffusion: the language reached cities first
Language extinction: the trade language replaced the others

why.correct: when a pidgin gains native speakers and grows into a full language, it has become a creole. That process is creolization.
options: Right: when a pidgin gains native speakers and grows into a full language, it has become a creole. That process is creolization.
Nothing in the stem judges a language. It describes a language changing as children learn it.
The stem describes a language growing in one place, not people carrying it there.
The stem says nothing about cities. It is about a contact language gaining native speakers.
Papua New Guinea still has hundreds of languages; Tok Pisin gaining native speakers is creolization.

items.q: English is widely used for international business, science and much of the internet. Which explanation best links this to globalization?
options: English is spoken at home by most people on Earth
Fast global links reward one shared language
English is a creole that formed on the internet
Globalization makes English the first language of each country
Globalization makes countries adopt one official language

why.correct: when people across the world trade, study and post online together, a shared language is useful. English filled that role, helped by the earlier spread of British and United States influence.
options: Most people speak another language at home; English is widely learned as a second language.
Right: when people across the world trade, study and post online together, a shared language is useful. English filled that role, helped by the earlier spread of British and United States influence.
English is not a creole of the internet; it spread through trade, empire, media and business.
English is widely used as a shared second language; most countries keep their own first languages.
Countries keep their own official languages; English is used beside them.

items.q: Greenland has its own parliament and runs most of its own affairs, but it is part of the Kingdom of Denmark, which handles its defense and foreign policy. What is Greenland?
options: An independent state
A stateless nation
A nation-state
A multistate nation
An autonomous region

why.correct: An autonomous region is a part of a state that governs many of its own affairs while the national government keeps powers such as defense. Greenland has had wide self-government since 2009.
options: Denmark still handles Greenland's defense and foreign policy.
Greenland is a place with a government, not a people without one.
Greenland is not an independent state; Denmark handles its defense and foreign policy.
That term describes a people spread over states, not a territory.
Right: Greenland governs most of its own affairs inside a larger state.

items.q: Soldiers from State M cross into State N and set up a base without State N's permission. Which principle has State M broken?
options: State N's sovereignty
State M's self-determination
State N's autonomy as a region
State N's devolution of power to State M
State M's nation-state status

why.correct: Each state has sovereignty over its own territory. Moving troops in without permission breaks it.
options: Right: State N alone has the right to control its territory.
Self-determination is a people's right to choose its status, not a right to enter another state.
State N is a state, not a region inside one.
Devolution is a state handing power to its own regions; here one state's soldiers entered another without permission.
Being a nation-state gives no right to enter another state.

items.q: A farmer puts up a fence and a "Private property: keep out" sign. At what scale is this an example of territoriality?
options: Local scale
Global scale
National scale
Global scale, because property laws exist worldwide
Regional scale

why.correct: Territoriality works at every scale: a fence and a sign claim control of one property, at the local scale.
options: Right: One person claims one small piece of land.
A fence around one property is not a claim over the world.
The claim is by one person, not a state.
The fence marks one farmer's land, so the territory claimed is local, whatever laws exist elsewhere.
The claim covers one property, not a region.

items.q: The Berlin Wall divided Berlin from 1961 to 1989. A few pieces still stand as a memorial. What type of boundary are those pieces part of?
options: Antecedent
Geometric
Relict
Consequent
Superimposed

why.correct: A relict boundary has stopped working but remains visible in the cultural landscape, as the Berlin Wall memorial does.
options: The wall was built through a crowded city.
The wall followed streets and old district lines, not a straight line.
Right: The wall no longer works as a border, but it still marks the landscape.
Germans lived on both sides; it did not follow a cultural line.
A superimposed boundary is forced on a landscape by an outside power and still works as a boundary; the wall pieces no longer divide anything.

items.q: Which mark is on a boundary that follows the crest of a high mountain range?
options: Mark A
Mark C
Mark E
Mark B
Mark D

why.correct: Chile and Argentina agreed in 1881 that their boundary would follow the highest peaks of the Andes (mark E).
options: Mark A is on a straight line across plains.
Mark C is on the line between Kenya and Tanzania near Kilimanjaro: mostly straight geometric segments, not the crest of a range.
Right: Mark E is on the Chile and Argentina boundary, which follows the high peaks of the Andes.
Mark B is on a former line in central Europe.
Mark D is on a boundary across mostly flat land and desert.

items.q: A boundary can fit more than one type. The one at mark A follows 49° N and was agreed in 1818 and 1846, before most settlers reached the land it crosses. Which pair of types fits it?
options: Geometric and antecedent
Relict and consequent
Physical and superimposed
Subsequent and relict
Consequent and superimposed

why.correct: The boundary at mark A is geometric (a line of latitude) and antecedent (drawn before most settlers arrived, though Indigenous peoples already lived there).
options: Right: It is a straight line of latitude, drawn before heavy settlement.
It still works, and it does not follow a cultural divide.
The line follows a parallel of latitude, not a river or ridge, and it was drawn before most settlers arrived, so it is geometric and antecedent.
It was drawn before most settlers arrived, and it still works.
It follows no cultural line, and the powers on both sides agreed it.

items.q: Since 1953, a strip of land about 4 km wide and about 250 km long has separated North Korea and South Korea, with no armed forces allowed inside it. What is this strip?
options: A territorial sea
A relict boundary
An exclusive economic zone
A demilitarized zone
A choke point

why.correct: The Korean Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) was set up by the 1953 armistice. It is one of the most closed boundaries in the world.
options: A territorial sea is the 12 nautical miles off a coast; this strip is on land, with armed forces kept out.
The Korean boundary still works as a closed border.
That is a sea zone, not a strip of land.
Right: A strip where armed forces are not allowed, set up by agreement after fighting.
A choke point is a narrow sea passage on a trade route.

items.q: After the 2020 US census, Texas gained two seats in the House of Representatives and Ohio lost one. Then Texas and Ohio drew new district lines. Which pair names these two steps in order?
options: Redistricting, then reapportionment
Gerrymandering, then demarcation
Redistricting, then gerrymandering
Packing, then cracking
Reapportionment, then redistricting

why.correct: Reapportionment shares the 435 House seats among the states by population after each census. Redistricting draws the district lines inside each state.
options: This reverses the order.
Gerrymandering is unfair line drawing, and demarcation marks a border on the ground.
Gaining and losing seats after the census is reapportionment; drawing new lines afterward is redistricting.
These are two methods of gerrymandering, not two stages.
Right: Seats are shared out among states first; then each state draws its districts.

items.q: In France, the national government in Paris sets what is taught in schools across the country, and regions carry out national policies. What form of government does this suggest?
options: Unitary
Federal
A confederation of regions
Autonomous
Multistate

why.correct: France is a common example of a unitary state: power is centered in Paris.
options: Right: Power is concentrated at the national level, in the capital.
In a federal state, the regions would have their own protected powers over schools.
In a confederation the regions hold most power; here Paris sets school content and the regions carry it out.
An autonomous region is a part of a state, not the state's system.
Multistate describes a nation spread across states.

items.q: Olives, grapes and citrus grow well in southern Spain, central Chile and coastal California. What do these places share that explains this kind of farming?
options: Heavy rain in each month of the year
Cold winters with deep snow and short summers
Long, cold winters with a short growing season
Thin, dry grassland too dry for any crop
Hot, dry summers and mild, rainy winters

why.correct: Climate shapes what can be grown. All three places have a Mediterranean climate, and farmers there grow drought-tolerant tree and vine crops, often with irrigation in summer.
options: Year-round rain describes tropical climates, such as Malaysia's, which suit plantation crops.
Short summers rule out slow-ripening crops like olives and citrus.
Olives and citrus are damaged by long hard frosts; all three places have mild, rainy winters and hot, dry summers.
Grassland too dry for crops supports herding or ranching, not orchards and vineyards.
Right: that is the Mediterranean climate, and the crops of Mediterranean agriculture can survive the summer drought.

items.q: Which is a common reason farm families choose to live in clustered villages instead of on their own scattered farms?
options: Sharing wells, defense, a market and a place of worship
Living in a village gives each family the largest possible farm
Each family wants to live right beside the fields it farms
The land was sold in separate squares to single families
Farmers want the shortest walk from their house to their crops

why.correct: Clustering trades a longer walk to the fields for shared water, safety, services and community.
options: Right: living close together makes it easier to share services and protect one another.
Living in a village does not make a farm larger; families cluster to share wells, defense, a market and a place of worship.
Living beside your own fields leads to dispersed settlement.
Separate squares sold to families led to dispersed farms in the US Midwest.
In a clustered village farmers walk farther to their fields: that is a cost of clustering.

items.q: After the First Agricultural Revolution, many people stopped moving to hunt and gather and lived in one place year-round. What best explains this change?
options: Fields and herds needed care, and harvests could be stored
People traded their crops for food from the Americas
Tractors made it possible to farm from a fixed home
Nomadic herding spread to each hearth area
Factories in towns offered steady wages to farm families

why.correct: Farming meant staying near fields and herds, and stored surpluses let villages grow. Permanent settlement followed.
options: Right: tending crops and storing food tied people to one place.
Farmers in Afro-Eurasia had no contact with the Americas at that time.
Tractors came thousands of years later.
Herding involves moving, the opposite of living in one place year-round.
Factories came with the Industrial Revolution, thousands of years after farming began.

items.q: In the four-field rotation used in Norfolk, England, in the 1700s, why was clover planted in one field each year?
options: It could be sold abroad for the highest price
It was the one crop that grew well in England's climate
It shaded the soil so weeds could not grow
It was harvested by the new steam-powered machines
It fed animals and put nitrogen back into the soil

why.correct: Rotating wheat, turnips, barley and clover kept every field busy and fed animals through winter. Clover added nitrogen, a nutrient wheat needs.
options: Clover was mostly grazed by farm animals, not sold abroad.
Wheat, barley and turnips grew there too.
Its main jobs were feed and restoring nitrogen to the soil.
Steam machines came later; clover was grown to feed animals and to put nitrogen back into the soil.
Right: clover fed livestock and restored the soil, so no field had to lie empty.

items.q: Which technology was NOT part of the Green Revolution that began in the 1960s?
options: High-yield varieties of rice and wheat
Synthetic fertilizers
Wider irrigation from wells and canals
Chemical pesticides
Crops given genes from another species in a lab

why.correct: Crops with genes inserted from another species are genetically modified organisms (GMOs). They were first sold commercially in the 1990s, decades after the Green Revolution began, so they were not part of it.
options: High-yield varieties, bred by crossing plants, were the heart of the Green Revolution.
Synthetic fertilizers were part of the package: the new seeds needed them to give large harvests.
Irrigation spread with the new seeds, which needed steady water.
Pesticides were part of the package that came with the new seeds.
Right: genetically modified crops came in the 1990s and are a separate technology.

items.q: What makes a high-yield variety different from the older local seeds it replaced?
options: Its genes were changed in a lab by inserting DNA from another species
It grows best on poor soil with little water
It needs no fertilizer or water to grow well
It grows tall so its stalks can reach more sunlight
It grows more grain per hectare when given water and fertilizer

why.correct: High-yield varieties were bred by crossing plants, not by lab gene changes. Short, stiff stalks held heavier grain, and yields depended on water and fertilizer.
options: That describes a GMO. Green Revolution seeds came from careful cross-breeding.
High-yield varieties give their large harvests when given water and fertilizer, which is why irrigation spread with them.
It needs more of both to reach its high yields.
Many were bred short, so heavy heads of grain would not knock the stalks over.
Right: high-yield varieties were bred to turn water and fertilizer into more grain.

items.q: Which farm types in the table are arranged as the von Thünen model predicts?
options: Cut flowers, dairy and wheat, from nearest to farthest
Ranching, wheat and dairy, from nearest to farthest
Wheat, dairy and wood lots, from nearest to farthest
Dairy, wood lots, wheat and ranching, from nearest to farthest
Wood lots, then dairy, then ranching, going from nearest to farthest

why.correct: Dairy (6 km), wood lots (18 km), wheat (40 km) and ranching (85 km) follow rings 1 to 4 of the model.
options: Cut flowers are the farthest of all, not the nearest.
That is the reverse of the table and of the model.
In the table dairy is nearest (6 km) and wheat farther out (40 km); this order reverses them.
Right: their distances rise in the model's ring order.
Dairy is nearer the capital than wood lots, as the model predicts.

items.q: Cut flowers are perishable and earn a lot per hectare, yet they are grown farthest from the capital. What best explains this exception?
options: Cold storage and air freight let them reach distant markets fresh
Cut flowers are heavy and cheap, like the products of the outer rings
Land far from the capital is the most expensive in the country
Flowers grow better in the colder climate of the outer rings
Flowers need no transport because they are sold at the farm

why.correct: Modern transport changes the model. Kenya, for example, flies cut flowers to Europe; the "market" for a specialty crop can be a continent away.
options: Right: refrigeration and fast transport break the link between perishability and distance.
Flowers are light and valuable, the opposite of outer-ring products.
Land usually gets cheaper with distance from the main market.
The table gives no climate for each ring; the reason in the table is how the flowers travel: refrigerated trucks and air freight.
The table says they travel by truck and air.

items.q: Which information would a researcher most need to judge how well the model fits Country A?
options: The capital's population in the year 1500
Maps of soil, slope and rivers in each area
The color of the flowers grown on each farm
The names of the families who own the dairies
The number of tractors sold in Country A each year

why.correct: Testing a model means checking its assumptions. Distances alone cannot tell you whether land is flat and even, as von Thünen assumed.
options: A population five centuries ago says little about land use now.
Right: the model assumes a flat, uniform plain; knowing where soils, slopes and rivers differ shows whether those assumptions hold.
Flower color does not test the model.
Ownership names do not affect the model's test.
Tractor sales say little about where each farm type sits; the model's isolated state assumes flat, even land, so soil, slope and rivers are the test.

items.q: Chicago grew from a small town in the 1830s to over one million people by 1890 (US census). Which change did the most to cause that growth?
options: Its marshy lakeside land was drained and turned into rich farms
Its winters grew much milder over those sixty years, drawing settlers
Rail lines met there, beside lake shipping
Gold was found in the hills around the town
It was chosen as the new national capital of the United States

why.correct: Transport changed Chicago's situation. As a meeting point of rail and lake routes, it handled the grain, cattle and lumber of the Midwest, and jobs followed.
options: Draining land changes the site a little but does not explain a boom.
Climate did not change enough to cause growth.
Right: new links made Chicago a hub, a better situation.
Chicago grew as a transport hub where rail met lake shipping, not from a gold rush.
Chicago has never been the national capital.

items.q: A family lives on a 2-hectare lot among horse farms, 70 kilometers from downtown Atlanta, and both parents drive into the metro area for work. What kind of place do they live in?
options: An edge city
An inner suburb
A boomburb inside the central city
An exurb
A central city

why.correct: A rural-looking area beyond the suburbs, where commuters live on large lots, is an exurb.
options: An edge city is an office and shopping center with many jobs.
Inner suburbs are close to the city and denser.
A boomburb is a fast-growing suburb, and the family lives far outside the built-up metro area, among farms.
Right: rural look, large lots, long commute: an exurb.
The central city is the old core, not 70 kilometers out.

items.q: A new kind of mobile payment appears first in Shanghai and Singapore, then in other large Asian cities, and years later in small towns. Which idea explains this path?
options: Contagious diffusion from village to village
Stimulus diffusion as each town invents its own payment system
Relocation diffusion by migrants leaving cities
Distance decay from the equator
Hierarchical diffusion down the urban hierarchy

why.correct: The idea moves from the top of the urban hierarchy down to smaller places, skipping the space between: hierarchical diffusion.
options: Contagious diffusion spreads to nearby places first, not to the biggest cities.
The same service spreads, and it moves from the largest cities down to small towns.
Nothing in the path shows people moving.
Distance decay is about distance between places, not from the equator.
Right: it spreads down the ladder of cities.

items.q: Which detail in the passage shows time-space compression?
options: Both sides sign the contract by video call in under an hour
The factory builds two million phones
The factory workers live near the factory they work in
The factory workers do not meet the people who decide their hours
The ships are booked by a port company

why.correct: Time-space compression is the shrinking of the time it takes to connect distant places. A deal across continents in under an hour shows it.
options: Right: fast links make distance matter less.
The size of an order says nothing about how fast places connect.
Living near work is distance at the local scale; time-space compression is about far places linked in less time.
Never meeting shows distance between workers and bosses, not faster links.
Booking ships is a task, not a change in how fast places connect.

items.q: What does the passage suggest about the role of world cities in globalization?
options: Factories decide where the world's money is lent
World cities make most of the goods that are traded
Globalization reduces the importance of cities
Each world city makes its own decisions with no tie to others
Decisions made in a few linked cities shape work in distant places

why.correct: The lending, legal work, advertising and shipping decisions are all made in world cities, and they set the hours of workers far away.
options: In the passage, the bank in London lends the money, not the factory.
In the passage, the phones are made in Viet Nam; the world cities provide decisions and services.
The passage shows cities at the center of the process.
The passage shows decisions in linked cities shaping distant work, so the cities are connected, not apart.
Right: world cities are command centers in a global network.

items.q: Which pair of scales does the passage link?
options: National laws and the prices of farm goods in one region
Local elections and the national borders they shape
Global decisions and local effects
Regional weather patterns and global shipping costs
Local weather and the national price of phones

why.correct: Firms and banks in world cities act at the global scale; the result is felt at the local scale, in the hours of one factory.
options: The passage mentions no national laws or farm prices.
The passage mentions no elections or borders.
Right: the passage ties global decisions to local outcomes.
The passage mentions no weather.
The passage says nothing about weather; it ties decisions made in world cities, at the global scale, to work in one place, the local scale.

items.q: Which change most weakens central place theory as a description of shopping in the 2020s?
options: Towns in the region have grown closer together
Most people in the region live on flat plains with even soil
Shoppers usually go to the nearest store that sells what they need
Small towns still sell everyday goods such as bread and gasoline
Online shopping replaces many trips

why.correct: The model assumes people travel to a central place to buy. Online shopping breaks the link between range and travel distance.
options: Closer towns still fit the theory's idea of market areas; it is online shopping that removes many trips to a central place.
A flat, even plain is the model's own assumption, so it would support it.
Shopping at the nearest store fits the model.
Everyday goods sold in small places fit the model.
Right: buying online ignores the model's travel assumption.

items.q: If Country A's cities followed the rank-size rule, about how many people would its third-largest city have?
options: About 600,000
About 180,000
About 133,000
About 300,000
About 400,000

why.correct: The rank-size rule puts the city of rank n at 1/n the size of the largest. The largest city has about 1,200,000 people, so the third-largest should have about 1,200,000 / 3 = 400,000.
options: About 600,000 is half the largest city: the rule's size for the second-largest city.
About 180,000 is the map's real third-largest city; the question asks what the rule predicts.
About 133,000 divides by 9, the rank squared; the rule divides by the rank.
About 300,000 divides by 4: the rule's size for the fourth-largest city.

items.q: Which statement best describes Country A's urban hierarchy on the map?
options: It has a primate city: the largest is more than four times the second
It follows the rank-size rule, with each city about the size the rule predicts
Its cities are about the same size in each of the eight provinces
Two cities of about equal size lead the hierarchy
The smallest cities are in the Capital Region and on the South Coast

why.correct: The largest city, about 1,200,000, is more than four times the second, about 260,000 on the South Coast. A city that much larger than the rest is a primate city.
options: Right: 1,200,000 is more than four times 260,000, the mark of a primate city.
The rule predicts about 600,000 for the second city; the map shows about 260,000, far smaller.
The circles differ a great deal: one is far larger than the other seven.
One city leads alone; the second is about a fifth of its size.
The largest cities are in the Capital Region and on the South Coast; the smallest are in the Northern Hills and Southern Forest.

items.q: Why did industrialization in the 1800s increase European control over colonies in Africa and Asia?
options: Factories needed raw materials and new buyers
Colonies in Africa and Asia had the newest factory machines
European factories ran short of workers and wanted farmland
Colonies had already built more factories than Europe
European governments wanted to slow their own factories

why.correct: Machines that make goods quickly need raw materials quickly and buyers for the goods, so industrial powers sought control of places that could supply both.
options: Right: the search for raw materials (cotton, rubber, palm oil) and markets fed colonialism and imperialism.
The machines and factories were in Europe; colonies supplied raw materials and bought factory goods.
The pull was raw materials and markets, not farmland for European factory workers.
Most colonies had few factories; they mainly supplied raw materials.
Governments backed factory growth; control of colonies helped it.

items.q: Shipping containers came into use in the 1950s and let cargo move from ship to train to truck without unpacking. What was one effect on where factories locate?
options: Cheaper shipping let factories locate far from buyers
Factories moved inland because ports closed to container ships
Factories had to move next to ports to use the containers
Transport costs rose instead
Ports stopped being break-of-bulk points as ships grew larger

why.correct: Containers cut the cost and time of moving goods, which weakened the pull of the market and let manufacturing spread to low-wage places worldwide.
options: Right: lower transport costs let firms chase cheap labor or land across oceans.
Ports grew with container ships; cheaper shipping let factories sit far from their buyers.
Containers move inland by train and truck too, so factories did not have to sit at ports.
Containers cut transport costs rather than raising them.
Cargo still changes from ship to train or truck at ports, just faster.

items.q: In Lagos, Nigeria, many people earn a living selling food and phone credit from street stalls, paid in cash and unregistered. What is this work an example of?
options: The quinary sector
The formal service sector
The informal sector
Gross national product
The Gender Inequality Index

why.correct: Unregistered, untaxed work paid in cash is the informal sector, which official income figures often miss.
options: Quinary jobs are top-level decisions; street selling is not.
The formal sector is registered and taxed; unregistered cash work from street stalls is informal.
Right: work that is not registered, taxed or counted by the government is informal.
GNP is a measure of output, not a kind of work.
GII is a measure of gaps between women and men, not a kind of work.

items.q: Two invented countries have about the same gross national income per person, but Country X has a much higher Human Development Index (HDI) than Country Y. What best explains the gap?
options: Country X has a larger population than Country Y
Country X earns more per person than Country Y
Country X has more land than Country Y
Country X has better health and education than Country Y
Country X has a larger primary sector than Country Y

why.correct: The HDI combines health (life expectancy), education (years of schooling) and income. With income about equal, the gap must come from health and education.
options: Population size is not part of the HDI.
The question says their income per person is about the same, so income cannot explain the gap.
Land area is not part of the HDI.
Right: health and education are the other two parts of the HDI.
The HDI does not measure economic sectors; a larger primary sector usually goes with lower development.

items.q: Since the 1980s, most workers in Bangladesh's garment factories have been women. Which statement gives both sides of what this has meant?
options: Women earn their own income, though pay is low and some sites have been unsafe
Women gained equal pay with men, and the factories have had no safety problems
Factory work ended the gap between women's and men's wages
Women lost paid work as men took the new factory jobs
The jobs moved women back into farming in rural Bangladesh

why.correct: The garment boom gave many women their own income and more say at home, but with low pay, long hours and dangerous buildings in some cases.
options: Right: the jobs brought income and some independence, alongside low pay and risks such as the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse.
The gender wage gap remained, and the 2013 Rana Plaza collapse killed more than 1,100 people.
Wages stayed low and a gap remained; the answer with both sides names income and the low pay and safety risks.
Most garment workers have been women, so women gained paid work.
The jobs are in factories, mostly around Dhaka, not in farming.

items.q: Which is the strongest criticism of Rostow's stages of economic growth?
options: It has too many stages
It assumes one Western path for all
It describes birth and death rates rather than the economy
It leaves out the stage of mass consumption
It says the world economy is one connected system

why.correct: Rostow assumed every country can follow the path of Britain and the United States, which ignores colonialism and global power.
options: The number of stages is not a weakness of the idea.
Right: it assumes one path for all and leaves out how richer countries shaped poorer ones.
That describes the demographic transition model.
Rostow's last stage is the age of high mass consumption, so the model includes it.
That is world system theory's claim, not Rostow's.

items.q: A student writes that invented Country P "moved up into the semiperiphery" after factories from wealthier countries opened there. Which model is the student using?
options: Rostow's stages of economic growth
Wallerstein's world-system theory
The demographic transition model
Least cost theory
The gravity model

why.correct: Core, semiperiphery and periphery are the three tiers of Wallerstein's world-system theory, which sees one connected world economy in which a country's place can change.
options: Rostow's model has five stages, from traditional society to high mass consumption; it has no semiperiphery.
Right: the semiperiphery is a tier of Wallerstein's world-system theory.
The demographic transition model describes birth and death rates, not places in the world economy.
Least cost theory explains where one factory locates, not a country's tier.
The gravity model predicts interaction between two places from their size and distance.

items.q: Costa Rica grows bananas in its warm lowlands, and Canada grows wheat and makes machines. Trade between them shows which idea most directly?
options: Complementarity: each supplies a need
Absolute advantage in each good for Canada
A single currency that Costa Rica and Canada both use
A tariff on bananas entering Canada
Structural adjustment by the IMF in Costa Rica

why.correct: Complementarity exists when one place supplies what another needs, here because the two climates differ.
options: Right: one place's supply meets another's need, largely because of climate.
Canada cannot grow bananas well, so it lacks an advantage in them.
Costa Rica uses the colón and Canada the Canadian dollar; each country supplying what the other needs is complementarity.
Nothing in the example is about a tax on imports.
Nothing in the example involves an IMF loan.

items.q: Toyota's factories in Japan have parts delivered only hours before they are used, so little stock sits in warehouses. What is this called?
options: Fordism
Break-of-bulk
Just-in-time delivery of factory parts
Agglomeration
Outsourcing of parts to other countries

why.correct: Delivering parts just when needed to keep little stock is just-in-time delivery.
options: Fordism is the mass production of identical goods on an assembly line, with large stocks.
Break-of-bulk is moving goods between kinds of transport.
Right: parts arrive just when needed, a key part of post-Fordism.
Agglomeration is firms clustering, not the timing of parts.
Outsourcing is about who makes the parts; delivering them hours before use is just-in-time.

items.q: On a map of Iowa, farmhouses are scattered evenly across the plains, while in a Dutch village the houses are packed around a central square. Which pair of terms fits?
options: Clustering in Iowa, dispersal in the village
Absolute distance in Iowa, relative distance in the village
Clustering in both places
Elevation in Iowa, distortion in the village
Dispersal in Iowa, clustering in the village

why.correct: Clustering means features are close together; dispersal means they are spread out.
options: This swaps the terms: the Iowa farmhouses are spread out, and the village houses are grouped.
Both places show how features are arranged, not how distance is measured.
Iowa's farmhouses are scattered evenly across the plains, which is dispersal.
Neither term describes how the houses are arranged.
Right: scattered, spread out features are dispersed; tightly grouped ones are clustered.

items.q: These data were collected by satellites far above Country A. What is this method called?
options: Remote sensing
Field observation in each province
A census of each household
Interviews with residents
A satellite navigation system

why.correct: Satellites and aircraft that record images or light from far away are doing remote sensing.
options: Right: remote sensing gathers data about places from a distance, usually by satellite or aircraft.
Field observation means going to the place and recording what you see.
A census counts people by asking them; these data were measured by satellite from far above.
Interviews ask people questions; satellites record light and images.
A satellite navigation system (such as GPS) tells a receiver where it is; it does not photograph the ground.

items.q: Which statement describes the pattern on this map?
options: Dispersed evenly, with about the same number of lights in each of the eight provinces
Clustered in the Capital Region and on the South Coast; few in the Western Uplands
Clustered in the Western Uplands and Northern Hills, with few near the South Coast
Spread in a line along the eastern border, with few in the center
Clustered in the north of Country A, with a few lights scattered along the coast

why.correct: Describe a dot map by naming where dots cluster and where they are sparse.
options: The dots are uneven: packed in the middle and south, sparse in the west.
Right: it names where the dots are packed and where they are few.
This reverses the map: the west has few dots.
The lights cluster in the Capital Region and on the South Coast, not along one border.
Most dots are in the Capital Region and on the South Coast, not the north.

items.q: A planner reads this map as a map of where people live. What is the best caution?
options: The satellite passed over at night, so it missed the people who were asleep indoors
A dot map shows counts, so it says nothing about where the lights are found
Lights show electricity, so villages without power may hold people the map misses
The dots show the height of the land, so they are about elevation, not people
Lights are counted by province, so the map hides the capital

why.correct: Remote sensing measures what it can see (here, light). Ask what that measure leaves out before using it for something else.
options: Satellites do record lights at night; that is how the map was made.
A dot map shows exactly where things are; that is its strength.
Right: light is a clue to where people are, not a count of them. Villages without electricity look empty from space.
The legend says the dots are bright lights, not height.
The dots are placed where the lights are; the caution is that light shows power use, so unlit villages are missed.

items.q: A family in Houston checks an official flood map before buying a house. What does this show about geographic data?
options: Flood maps are useful at the global scale alone
Flood maps are made for government planners, so the family misused one
Individuals use geographic data for personal decisions too
A flood map is qualitative data, so it is less reliable than a census
The family made a national decision about the whole country's floods

why.correct: Geographic data shape decisions by individuals too: where to buy, rent or travel.
options: A flood map for one house is local data, used here for a family decision.
Flood maps are published for the public to use.
Right: people use maps and data to decide where to live, travel or work.
A flood map shows mapped risk zones; it is not a set of interviews.
One house in one city is a local, personal decision.

items.q: Singapore is a city-state on a small, low island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula. Which statement describes Singapore's situation rather than its site?
options: It sits beside the Strait of Malacca, a main shipping route between oceans
It is built on a low, mostly flat main island
Much of its land was made by filling in the sea
Its climate is hot and wet in each month of the year
Its absolute location is about 1° N, 104° E

why.correct: Situation is a place's location relative to other places. Singapore's position on a busy shipping route between the Indian Ocean and the Pacific is its situation.
options: Right: its position on a route between other places is its situation.
The shape and height of the island are features of the place itself: its site.
Land made by filling in the sea is part of its site, the physical ground the city stands on.
Climate is a physical feature of the place itself, part of its site.
Latitude and longitude give absolute location, not situation.

items.q: At the national scale, Australia looks almost empty. Which statement describes its population distribution at a more detailed scale?
options: Most Australians live on farms spread across the interior
Australians are spread fairly evenly across the interior and the coasts of the country
Most Australians live in the dry center of the country
Australia has no clusters of people
Most live in east and southeast coastal cities; the dry interior is nearly empty

why.correct: One national number hides a strong pattern. Most Australians live near the east and southeast coasts, where rain falls and the large cities are; the dry interior is nearly empty.
options: Australia is highly urban, and its people cluster in east and southeast coastal cities.
the dry interior has very few people.
the center is dry and has few people; the coasts are where most live.
Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane are large clusters on the coast.
Right: this names where people are and where they are not.

items.q: A government plans to build a new hospital. Its province has very low density, with villages far apart. Which problem is most likely?
options: Many patients would live far away, so trips would be long
The hospital would be too crowded on its first day of opening
Housing near the hospital would become too expensive for its nurses and other workers
The hospital would have too many staff for so few homes
There would be too much traffic on roads near the hospital

why.correct: Low density raises the cost of services per person and the distance to them. High density brings crowding, traffic and high housing costs.
options: Right: low density spreads people out, so a single hospital is far from many of them.
crowding is a problem of high density.
high housing prices are usually a problem of crowded places.
Staffing is a planning choice; the problem low density causes is the long distance patients travel.
heavy traffic comes with high density.

items.q: The baby boom in the United States lasted from 1946 to 1964. In a pyramid of the United States for 2020, where would the baby boomers appear?
options: As a wide band at ages 0 to 19
As a wide band at ages 30 to 44, the middle of the pyramid
As a wide band at ages 55 to 74
As a narrow band at ages 80 and over
As a narrow band at ages 0 to 4

why.correct: A cohort moves up the pyramid as it ages. A large birth cohort shows as a bulge that climbs about one bar every five years.
options: those are people born from 2001 to 2020.
those were born from 1976 to 1990.
Right: people born 1946 to 1964 were 56 to 74 years old in 2020.
the boomers were all younger than 75 in 2020.
People born from 1946 to 1964 were 56 to 74 in 2020, so they form a wide band in late middle age.

items.q: In Country Q, women outnumber men in the 80 and over group. Which statement best explains this?
options: More girls than boys are born each year in most countries
On average, women live longer than men
More men than women are counted in the 80 and over group
Older women are counted twice in many censuses
Older men in Country Q have moved abroad in large numbers

why.correct: Women live longer than men on average in almost every country, so the sex ratio falls at older ages and the female side of the top bars is longer.
options: slightly more boys are usually born, about 105 for every 100 girls.
Right: more women survive to the oldest ages, so the female bar is longer.
The pyramid shows the reverse: the female bar is longer at 80 and over.
there is no such counting rule.
the pyramid cannot show this, and men living shorter lives is the usual reason.

items.q: Which question can Country Q’s national pyramid NOT answer?
options: Whether children or adults aged 50 to 54 are more numerous in Country Q
Whether women outnumber men in the oldest group
Which cities in Country Q have the most older people
Whether more people are aged 45 to 49 than 0 to 4
Which age group is the largest in Country Q

why.correct: A national pyramid describes the whole country’s age and sex structure. It cannot show where in the country each group lives, or why the pattern formed: those need data at another scale.
options: the bars show this: the 50-54 bars are longer.
the 80+ bars show more women than men.
Right: a national pyramid has no data on where people live inside the country.
The pyramid shows both bars, so it can answer this; it cannot show where in Country Q older people live.
the longest bars show the largest cohort.

items.q: Invented Country K has a crude birth rate of 32 and a crude death rate of 7 per 1,000 people a year. With no migration, about how many years will its population take to double?
options: About 2.8 years
About 25 years
About 28 years
About 22 years
About 70 years

why.correct: The rate of natural increase is (32 - 7) / 10 = 2.5%. By the rule of 70, the doubling time is 70 / 2.5 = 28 years.
options: 2.8 years divides 70 by 25, the gap per 1,000; turn it into a percent first (2.5%).
25 is the gap between the rates per 1,000 people, not a number of years.
Right: RNI = 2.5%, and 70 / 2.5 = 28 years.
About 22 years divides 70 by 3.2, the birth rate alone; deaths must be taken away first.
70 is the rule's number before dividing by the growth rate.

items.q: A family leaves a village in Guatemala planning to reach the United States. In Mexico City they find steady work and good schools, and they stay. What does this show?
options: An intervening obstacle
Chain migration
Transhumance
Forced migration
An intervening opportunity

why.correct: An intervening opportunity is a chance along the way, here work and schools in Mexico City, that leads a migrant to stop short of the planned destination.
options: An obstacle would block or slow the move; this family found something good and chose to stay.
Chain migration is following relatives or friends who moved earlier; nothing here says the family joined anyone.
Transhumance is the seasonal movement of herders and their animals.
The family chose to move and chose to stay, so the move is voluntary.
Right: work and schools on the way led them to stop: an intervening opportunity.

items.q: At the council meeting, residents asked for different things. What does this show about the political effects of migration?
options: Residents of the town agree on how to respond to migration
Migration has no effect on politics in small towns
Migration can bring debate over services and visas
The local council decides how many work visas the country gives
Migration changes the borders of the town

why.correct: Migration often brings political debate at several scales: local (classes, schools, housing) and national (visa numbers and immigration policy). Our job is to describe the debate, not to take a side.
options: some want more help, others fewer visas.
the report shows a political debate in a small town.
Right: residents disagree about how to respond.
the residents asked the national government, which sets visa numbers.
Migration changes who lives in the town, not its borders; the meeting shows debate over services and visas.

items.q: Riverton’s growth is described at the local scale. Which statement links it to another scale?
options: Most new workers in Riverton came from nearby farms
Riverton’s school will add classrooms next year
Two new grocery stores opened in the town center in the last few years
The meat-packing plant is in Riverton
National visa rules shape how many workers reach the town

why.correct: Effects connect across scales. A national immigration policy (national scale) changes how many workers a plant can hire (local scale).
options: Moves from nearby farms stay at the local scale; national visa rules link the town to the national scale.
that stays at the local scale.
that stays at the local scale.
that names a place but links no scales.
Right: a national policy shapes a local outcome.

items.q: A national survey of invented Country A finds that most teenagers stream the same few shows. In one mountain province, though, most families still sing traditional work songs at harvest. What does comparing the two scales show?
options: Folk culture has disappeared everywhere in Country A
The national survey proves the mountain province has no popular culture
Popular culture leads nationally; folk culture survives locally
Scale makes no difference to what the data show
Folk culture leads nationally; popular culture survives locally

why.correct: national data hide local differences. At the national scale one pattern wins; at the local scale a folk tradition still stands out.
options: The mountain province still sings traditional songs, so folk culture has not disappeared.
The survey describes the country as a whole. Families in the province may stream shows and also keep their songs.
Right: national data hide local differences. At the national scale one pattern wins; at the local scale a folk tradition still stands out.
The point of the example is that the local scale reveals a pattern the national scale hides.
This reverses the two scales: the national survey shows popular culture, and the province keeps a folk tradition.

items.q: On the Navajo Nation, which spreads across parts of Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, some families still build hogans, many-sided homes (often six or eight sides) whose doors face east toward the rising sun. What does a hogan show on the cultural landscape?
options: A popular culture trend copied from shopping malls
A building style set by the dry climate of the Southwest
A physical feature shaped by wind and erosion
A postmodern style that mixes many building eras
A traditional design carrying the beliefs of a people

why.correct: the shape and the east-facing door are choices made by Navajo culture, so the building marks Navajo beliefs and traditions on the land.
options: Hogans follow a long-standing Navajo design, not a fast-changing trend.
Climate alone does not explain the many sides or the east-facing door; those carry the beliefs of the Diné (Navajo) people.
People build hogans, so they are part of the cultural landscape, not the physical one.
A hogan keeps one long-standing design, so it is traditional architecture.
Right: the shape and the east-facing door are choices made by Navajo culture, so the building marks Navajo beliefs and traditions on the land.

items.q: Which feature in the 2020 panel is a mark left by an earlier group of people?
options: The brick mill and its smokestack
The glass tower beside the old mill building
The river that flows past the mill
The riverside path along the water
The cafe sign on the front of the old mill

why.correct: the mill was built in the mill-town period and is still standing, reused for a new purpose. Old marks staying on the land is what sequent occupance describes.
options: Right: the mill was built in the mill-town period and is still standing, reused for a new purpose. Old marks staying on the land is what sequent occupance describes.
The tower appears only in the 2020 panel, so it is a new mark, not an earlier one.
The river is a physical feature, not a mark left by people; the brick mill and smokestack are left from the 1920 period.
The path appears only in the 2020 panel. It is a mark of the latest period.
The sign was added in the latest period, even though the building it hangs on is older.

items.q: What idea do the three panels show together?
options: Environmental determinism: the river decides how people use the site
Sequent occupance: each group leaves marks that later groups reuse
Ethnocentrism: each new group judges the group before it
Placelessness: the riverbank looks like any other place
Folk culture: one small group keeps the same ways for centuries

why.correct: the site carries layers from a fishing camp, a mill town and a modern city. Each period adds to, or reuses, what came before.
options: The river stays the same in all three panels, yet the land use changes three times. People made different choices.
Right: the site carries layers from a fishing camp, a mill town and a modern city. Each period adds to, or reuses, what came before.
The panels show land use changing, not any group judging another culture.
Each period leaves a distinct mark that later groups reuse, so the panels show sequent occupance.
The uses change completely between panels, so this is not one unchanging tradition.

items.q: Many people in Catalonia, Spain, share the Catalan language, and debates about Catalonia's place in Spain have divided the country. What does this show about centripetal and centrifugal forces?
options: A shared language can act as a centripetal force alone
Centrifugal forces appear mainly at the global scale
Language divides people at the local scale alone
One trait can unite at one scale and divide at another
Language plays no part in uniting or dividing people

why.correct: Catalan pulls people together at the regional scale of Catalonia, while the same identity pulls against the rest of Spain at the national scale.
options: The example shows the language uniting Catalonia but dividing Spain, so it acts as both.
The division here is within one country, at the national scale.
Catalan unites many people within Catalonia, while debates about the region divide Spain: one trait works differently at each scale.
Right: Catalan pulls people together at the regional scale of Catalonia, while the same identity pulls against the rest of Spain at the national scale.
Language is one of the strongest forces that unite or divide.

items.q: Without internet or phones, a new craft style spreads by contagious diffusion and is common near its hearth but rare far away. Which Unit 1 idea explains why it is rare far away?
options: Possibilism: people far away chose to reject the style
Environmental determinism: climate blocks the style far away
Sequent occupance: later groups covered the style over time
Distance decay: contact falls as distance grows
Hierarchical diffusion: the style reached big cities first

why.correct: the farther a place is from the hearth, the less contact it has, so contagious diffusion weakens with distance.
options: The stem gives no choice by distant people; it is about how little contact reaches them.
Nothing in the stem ties the style to climate. Distance limits contact.
Sequent occupance is about layers in one place, not about how far a trait spreads.
Right: the farther a place is from the hearth, the less contact it has, so contagious diffusion weakens with distance.
A style spreading by contagion goes to nearby places first, with no order of places by size.

items.q: Papermaking began in China and reached Samarkand, in Central Asia, by about the 700s, then Baghdad and later Europe. Which historical cause best explains this spread?
options: European colonial rule over China in the 700s
Streaming video teaching people how to make paper
Creole languages formed in Caribbean ports
Trade routes linking China with lands to the west
Relocation diffusion by Chinese settlers in Europe in the 700s

why.correct: the Silk Roads carried goods, people and skills between China and lands to the west, so papermaking spread along them.
options: No European power ruled China in the 700s. Trade routes, not colonies, carried papermaking west.
Streaming video did not exist in the 700s.
Caribbean creoles came centuries later and have nothing to do with papermaking.
Right: the Silk Roads carried goods, people and skills between China and lands to the west, so papermaking spread along them.
Papermaking passed along trade routes through Central Asia and Southwest Asia, not by Chinese settlement in Europe.

items.q: A family that moved from the Philippines to Toronto, Canada, video-calls relatives every week, watches Filipino shows online and cooks Filipino food. How does technology affect their culture?
options: It helps them keep culture from home
It replaces their culture with Canadian folk culture
It forces them to stop speaking their home language
It ends their contact with the Philippines
It turns their culture into the physical landscape

why.correct: fast, cheap links let migrants keep their language, food and ties alive across great distance.
options: Right: fast, cheap links let migrants keep their language, food and ties alive across great distance.
Weekly calls and Filipino shows keep ties to home; technology here helps them keep their culture.
The calls and shows give them more chances to use their language, not fewer.
Weekly calls show more contact, not less.
Culture is learned and shared; technology does not make it physical.

items.q: The owner's children speak English at school and Vietnamese at home, and still bake for Tết. Which term best describes this?
options: Assimilation
Acculturation
Ethnocentrism
Environmental determinism
Hierarchical diffusion

why.correct: Acculturation is taking on traits of another culture while keeping one's own. The children use English outside the home and keep Vietnamese and the Tết baking.
options: Assimilation is giving up the old culture for the new one; the children keep Vietnamese and Tết.
Right: they adopt English and keep their own language and festival.
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own; nothing in the passage judges anyone.
