Environmental determinism says the physical environment decides culture; the passage is about people and choices.
Hierarchical diffusion is spread from larger places or people of power downward; the passage describes one family.

items.q: Koreans and Kurds both live in more than one state. What is the key difference between them?
options: Kurds live in more states than Koreans, so Kurds alone count as a nation
Koreans have states of their own; Kurds have none
Koreans are a nation-state and Kurds are a multinational state
Kurds live on a peninsula and Koreans do not
Koreans are a stateless nation; Kurds have two states

why.correct: Both are multistate nations. Koreans form the majority in North Korea and South Korea, while the Kurds have no independent state, so the Kurds are also a stateless nation.
options: Both groups are nations; the number of states does not decide it.
Right: Both are spread across states, but only the Kurds lack a state of their own.
Those terms describe states, not peoples spread across states.
The Kurds' homeland is inland, and location does not define these terms.
It is the reverse: Koreans have two states on the peninsula, and Kurds have none.

items.q: In 1964, the Organization of African Unity agreed that its members would respect the borders they had at independence. How did this decision shape the map of Africa?
options: Borders were redrawn to give each ethnic group its own state
Each colonial power redrew the borders after leaving
Most colonial-era borders stayed in place after independence
African states merged into one large federation
Colonial powers kept control of border areas

why.correct: Respecting the borders held at independence kept the colonial outlines on the map, even where they split or grouped peoples.
options: The decision did the opposite: it froze the inherited borders.
The 1964 agreement kept colonial-era borders in place; it did not redraw them.
Right: States agreed not to redraw the borders they inherited.
No such merger took place.
The decision was made by independent African states.

items.q: An oil tanker leaves a port on the Persian Gulf (also called the Arabian Gulf) for the Indian Ocean. Which marked choke point must it pass?
options: A
B
C
D
E

why.correct: E is the Strait of Hormuz, the only sea route out of the Persian Gulf, so every tanker leaving the Gulf passes it.
options: A is the Strait of Gibraltar, at the western end of the Mediterranean, far from the Gulf.
B is the Bosporus, between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean.
C is the Suez Canal, between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.
D is the Bab-el-Mandeb, at the southern end of the Red Sea; a tanker from the Gulf need not enter the Red Sea.
Right: E, the Strait of Hormuz, is the mouth of the Persian Gulf.

items.q: How is neocolonialism different from colonialism?
options: Neocolonialism is direct rule; colonialism works through trade and money alone
Neocolonialism works through money and influence; colonialism is direct rule
Neocolonialism happened before the 1500s; colonialism happened after 1945
Neocolonialism needs settlers; colonialism uses no people from outside
Neocolonialism and colonialism are two names for direct rule

why.correct: Colonialism is direct control and often settlement. Neocolonialism is indirect influence over a sovereign state, through loans, trade, currency or investment.
options: This swaps the two.
Right: The outside power shapes decisions without governing the territory.
Colonialism came first; neocolonialism describes the period after independence.
Settlement is a feature of some colonialism.
Neocolonialism is indirect control through money and influence, so the two are different.

items.q: How is a delimited boundary different from a demarcated one?
options: Delimited is drawn on a map; demarcated is marked on the ground
Delimited is marked on the ground; demarcated is drawn on a map
Delimited is a natural boundary; demarcated is a geometric one
Delimited is defined in a treaty; demarcated is guarded by soldiers
Delimited is a land boundary; demarcated is a sea boundary

why.correct: States define a boundary in words, delimit it on maps, demarcate it with markers on the ground and administer it day to day.
options: Right: Maps come first, then posts, fences or walls on the ground.
This swaps the two.
Natural and geometric are kinds of lines; delimiting and demarcating are steps in drawing and marking one.
Defining in words comes before delimiting; guarding is administration.
Both words apply on land and at sea.

items.q: A city council is elected from eight districts, and the city redraws them after the census. At which scale is this redistricting?
options: Global scale
Local scale
National scale
Regional scale
Continental scale

why.correct: Redistricting happens at several scales: US House districts inside a state, state legislative districts, and city council and school board districts at the local scale.
options: The districts lie inside one city.
Right: City council districts divide one city.
The districts cover one city, not a country.
One city is smaller than a region.
A city council's districts are inside one city: the local scale.

items.q: Which pattern does the table show?
options: Mareh-speaking regions are poorer, with less electricity
Income and electricity are about equal in each of the regions
The Mareh-speaking regions have the highest incomes
The Coast is poorer than the Desert
The Capital region has the least electricity

why.correct: Read across the rows: the Sell-speaking Capital and Coast are richer and better served than the Mareh-speaking Plateau and Desert.
options: Right: The Plateau and Desert have the lowest incomes and electricity shares.
Incomes range from 4,000 to 24,000 dollars.
They have the lowest.
The Coast earns 18,000 dollars, the Desert 4,000.
The Capital region has the most: 99% of homes. The Mareh-speaking Plateau and Desert have the least.

items.q: Why could the pattern in the table become a strong centrifugal force in Country S?
options: Language differences fade where electricity reaches homes
The four regions share one language
The richest region of the country lies far from the capital
Electricity reaches nearly each home in the country
Poverty and language overlap, feeding blame of the center

why.correct: Uneven development is centrifugal, and more so when it lines up with ethnicity or language: the poorer group can come to see the state as serving someone else.
options: Nothing in the table shows language fading; poverty and language overlap, which can feed a sense of being left behind.
Two languages are listed.
The capital region is the richest.
Only 30% of homes in the Desert have it.
Right: When an ethnic divide matches a wealth divide, grievances build along one line.

items.q: Which question can the table NOT answer?
options: Which region has the lowest income per person
Which region has the highest income per person
Which language is spoken in the Plateau
Whether Mareh speakers want to leave
What share of Coast homes have electricity

why.correct: Data on income and services can suggest a reason for division, but they cannot show what people think. That would need a survey or a vote.
options: The Desert, at 4,000 dollars.
The table gives income per person for each region, so it can answer this.
The table lists Mareh for the Plateau.
Right: The table shows income, power and language, not what people want.
The table gives 95% for the Coast.

items.q: Market gardens grow fruit and vegetables that spoil quickly, such as lettuce, tomatoes and strawberries. Why are they usually located near large cities, such as the greenhouses near Rotterdam?
options: Fruit and vegetables need the larger fields found near cities
Land near cities is cheaper than land farther away from them
Cities have the dry summers these crops need
Herds need to graze close to the market
Fresh produce needs to reach shoppers before it spoils

why.correct: Market gardening (also called truck farming) is intensive and sits close to its market because its products are perishable and in high demand.
options: Land near cities is costly, so fields there are small; market gardens sit close because the produce spoils.
Land near cities usually costs more, which is one reason market gardens use it so intensively.
Market gardens grow in many climates; greenhouses even make their own.
Market gardening grows crops, not herds.
Right: perishable crops need a short trip to the people who buy them.

items.q: A deed from 1790 in Kentucky marks a farm boundary at "the large oak by the creek." Which problem is most likely to arise from this metes and bounds description?
options: The farm is split into long lots that run back from the creek
The farm is forced into a square exactly one mile on each side
The boundary becomes unclear when the tree dies or the creek moves
The farm has no access to water because it is far from the creek
Houses on the farm line up along a road in a linear pattern

why.correct: Metes and bounds relies on landmarks. When landmarks change, neighbors may disagree on where the line is: a known limit of the method.
options: Long lots are a different survey system; the problem here is a boundary tied to a tree and a creek that can change.
A fixed square of one mile is a section in township and range, not metes and bounds.
Right: features that change or vanish make metes and bounds lines hard to find, which leads to disputes.
The deed puts the boundary at the creek, so the farm touches it.
The deed describes a boundary, not where houses stand.

items.q: Farming spread from the Fertile Crescent into Europe over thousands of years, as each generation of farmers cleared land a little farther from the last. Which type of diffusion is this?
options: Relocation diffusion, carried by ship across an ocean
Expansion diffusion, spreading from place to place
Hierarchical diffusion, moving first between large cities
Contagious diffusion by ship between Europe's large cities
Stimulus diffusion, changing into a new practice

why.correct: Farming spread outward from its hearth to neighboring areas, which is expansion diffusion (contagious). The Columbian Exchange, by contrast, carried crops across an ocean: relocation diffusion.
options: Relocation diffusion moves an idea with people to a distant place; here farming crept outward step by step.
Right: farming spread outward from its hearth while staying strong at home, a form of contagious expansion diffusion.
Cities did not yet exist across Europe; farming spread through neighboring lands.
Farming moved over land, generation by generation, from place to place: expansion diffusion.
The same crops and practices spread, not just an idea that was changed.

items.q: According to the passage, which process brought the potato from the Andes to Ireland?
options: The Green Revolution of the 1960s
The First Agricultural Revolution
Contagious diffusion across land from the Andes to Ireland
The Columbian Exchange
Stimulus diffusion of a farming idea, not the plant itself

why.correct: The Columbian Exchange moved plants, animals and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia after 1492. The potato is one of its best-known crops.
options: The potato reached Ireland centuries before the Green Revolution, through the Columbian Exchange.
That is the first domestication of plants and animals, thousands of years earlier, in the Andes itself.
An ocean lies between them; the potato crossed it by ship.
Right: after 1492, ships carried crops such as the potato from the Americas to Europe.
The passage says the plant itself was carried to Europe.

items.q: Based on the passage, why was the blight so deadly in Ireland?
options: Many families depended on one kind of potato for most of their food
Irish farmers grew many kinds of potato, so the blight had many targets
The potato could not grow in Ireland's cool, wet climate
The potato had been brought to Ireland just a few years before 1845
The blight spread to Ireland from the United States

why.correct: Depending on one crop is risky. When blight struck the one potato variety most poor families relied on, their main food source collapsed.
options: Right: when the one crop failed, those families had little else to eat.
Families depended on one kind, which is why one disease could ruin most of the food supply.
The passage says the potato grew well in Ireland's climate.
It arrived in the late 1500s, more than 200 years earlier.
The passage does not say that; it says many Irish people later moved to the United States.

items.q: In the passage, the famine led more than 1 million people to leave Ireland. For those migrants, what was the famine?
options: A pull factor
A push factor
A form of step migration inside Ireland
An intervening opportunity
A form of internal migration

why.correct: A famine at home is a push factor. The passage links a farming event to a migration flow, a cross-unit link the exam often asks for.
options: A pull factor draws people to a destination; the famine pushed them from Ireland.
Right: the famine was a condition at the origin that drove people away.
Leaving Ireland is international migration, and the famine pushed people out: a push factor.
An intervening opportunity is a chance found along the way that ends a move early.
Leaving Ireland for the United States is international migration.

items.q: In the 1700s and 1800s, landowners in England fenced shared village fields and commons into private farms. What was a major effect of this enclosure?
options: Village fields were split into narrow strips running from rivers
Farmers returned to hunting and gathering on the commons
Small farmers gained the commons as private land
Each family received a square section of 640 acres
Larger farms adopted new methods, but many small farmers lost land

why.correct: Enclosure had positive and negative effects: more productive farms, and also landless families who moved to towns for work.
options: Strips from rivers are long lots, a French survey method in North America.
Enclosure ended shared use of the commons; it did not bring back foraging.
The commons were fenced into larger private farms, and many small farmers lost access to them.
Square sections are part of the US township and range survey.
Right: enclosure allowed new rotations and breeding on larger farms, and it pushed many rural families off the land.

items.q: How does the Green Revolution challenge Malthusian theory?
options: It proved that population grows faster than food
Technology raised food output faster than population grew
It stopped population growth in South Asia
It showed that population cannot grow without new seeds
It showed that famines are caused by too few people

why.correct: Malthus (1798) argued food grows slowly. The Green Revolution raised yields so much that food per person rose in many countries. Neo-Malthusians reply that it depends on water and fuel that may run short.
options: That is Malthus's claim; the Green Revolution is evidence against it.
Right: Malthus expected food supply to grow slowly; new seeds and inputs made it grow quickly.
Population kept growing; food grew faster.
Population grew before and during the Green Revolution; what it challenged was Malthus's claim that food cannot keep up.
Malthus linked famines to too many people for the food; the Green Revolution showed food supply can rise.

items.q: In Mato Grosso, Brazil, huge farms grow soybeans across thousands of hectares. What is one risk of this monocropping?
options: The farm is too small to sell its crop to buyers
The soybeans spoil before they reach a market
The farm grows too many different crops to manage
A pest or price drop can hit the whole harvest at once
The farm moves to a new forest plot after a few years

why.correct: Monocropping is efficient for machines and sales, but it puts all the risk on one crop and can wear down soils without rotation.
options: These farms are among the largest in the world and sell nearly all they grow.
Dry soybeans store well; the risk of one crop is that one pest or price drop hits everything.
Monocropping is the opposite: one crop.
Right: with one crop, a disease, pest or fall in price affects everything the farm grows.
That describes shifting cultivation, not large commercial soy farms.

items.q: Starting in the 1980s, China slowly loosened rules that had made it hard for rural people to move to cities. What effect did this most likely have?
options: A move of most factories from cities to rural villages
A faster rise in the urban share
More people moving from the big coastal cities back to inland farms
Fewer factory jobs in cities, as workers left for the countryside
A sudden fall in China's total population as families moved abroad

why.correct: When a policy that held people in villages eases, people respond to city pull factors, and the urban share climbs.
options: Loosening the rules let rural people move to city jobs, raising the urban share.
Right: easing limits on moving lets migration, and so urbanization, speed up.
Easing limits on moving to cities would not push people back to farms.
City jobs grew in this period; the policy did not cut them.
A migration rule moves people within the country; it does not shrink the total.

items.q: Tysons, Virginia, outside Washington, D.C., grew from a rural crossroads in the 1960s into a large cluster of offices and shopping malls along highways, with more jobs than residents. What is Tysons?
options: An exurb
A central business district
A squatter settlement
An edge city
A primate city

why.correct: An edge city is a large node of offices and shopping that grows at the edge of a metro area along highways, often with more jobs than homes.
options: An exurb is a low-density area of homes beyond the suburbs, with few jobs of its own.
The central business district of the metro area is downtown Washington, D.C.
A squatter settlement is housing built without legal title, usually at the edge of a city in a periphery country.
Right: offices and malls at the edge of the metro area, along highways, with more jobs than residents.
A primate city is a country's largest city, far larger than the next; Tysons is part of one metro area.

items.q: A bank board in London decides to stop lending to a textile company, and a factory in Dhaka cuts 2,000 jobs. Which statement describes the scales involved?
options: A decision at the local scale has an effect at the global scale
A decision at the global scale has an effect at the local scale
Both the decision and the effect are at the national scale
A decision at the regional scale has no effect elsewhere
The scale is unclear unless a map of the bank and factory is given

why.correct: The bank acts in the world economy, a global-scale decision; the job losses fall on one factory, a local-scale effect.
options: This reverses the direction: the decision is global and the effect local.
Right: global decision, local effect.
The decision crosses countries, so it is not national.
The London decision cut jobs in Dhaka, so it did have an effect, at the local scale.
The scale of a process can be named from what it reaches.

items.q: Which statement best describes the pattern of city sizes on the map of Country A?
options: Cities of about the same size in each of the eight provinces
Two equal cities, one in the north and one in the south
The largest cities lined up along the northern border
One very large city, in the Capital Region
City size rising steadily from the west coast to the east

why.correct: The Capital Region's circle (900 thousand) is about four times the next largest, on the South Coast (220 thousand). The rest are small.
options: The capital's circle is far larger than any other.
The map shows one city far larger than the rest, in the Capital Region.
The Northern Hills has the smallest circle.
Right: one dominant city, a primate pattern at the national scale.
Sizes do not rise from west to east; the Capital Region is the peak.

items.q: According to the gravity model, which pair of cities on the map should interact the most?
options: The Northern Hills city and the Southern Forest city
The Capital Region city and the Central Valley city
The Northern Hills city and the Western Uplands city
The Western Uplands city and the Lake District city
The Northern Hills city and the South Coast city

why.correct: Interaction grows with population and falls with distance. The capital is the largest city on the map and the Central Valley city is a neighbor, so this pair scores highest.
options: Both are small and they sit at opposite ends of the country.
Right: the largest city and a close neighbor.
Both are small (60,000 and 100,000 people), so the model expects little interaction; it favors large cities close together.
Both are small and on opposite sides of the country.
One is the smallest city and they are far apart.

items.q: What is one limit of using this map to test the gravity model?
options: It shows no flows between the cities
It shows flows of people between cities but not their sizes
It uses real census data, so it may be out of date by now
It gives the distance between the cities in kilometers
It shows the cities at the global scale rather than in one country

why.correct: The gravity model predicts interaction. To test it you need data on flows (trips, calls, trade), and the map shows only sizes.
options: Right: no flow data, so no test of the prediction.
The circles show sizes; no flows are drawn.
The map is invented data for practice.
Distances can be measured from a map; the limit is that it shows no flows of people or goods to test against.
The map shows one country by province, a national view.

items.q: Metro Los Angeles has many separate centers: a downtown, a port, an airport district, university areas and film studios. Which model fits best?
options: Multiple nuclei
Concentric zone
Central place theory
Sector
Latin American city

why.correct: Several separate centers of different kinds, each drawing its own land uses, are the multiple nuclei model.
options: Right: many nuclei of different kinds.
The concentric zone model has one center.
Central place theory spaces towns and their market areas across a region; it is not a model of land use inside one city. Many separate specialized centers is multiple nuclei.
The sector model has one center with wedges.
The Latin American model has one CBD with a spine.

items.q: Detroit lost more than half its population between the 1950 and 2020 US censuses, and many houses were torn down. Which stage of the cycle of development does this show?
options: Redevelopment of the city's oldest blocks into towers
Infilling, adding new homes on empty lots
Early growth of new homes on open farmland
Decline, leaving vacant land
The rise of a new CBD on the edge of the city

why.correct: Losing people and jobs, then demolishing empty houses, is the decline stage. The vacant land can later be reused.
options: Detroit lost people and houses were torn down: decline, not redevelopment.
Infilling adds buildings; here they were removed.
Detroit was built up long before; this is the later decline.
Right: decline leaves empty lots.
A shrinking city is not forming a new CBD.

items.q: In 2007, Kenya's M-Pesa service let people send and store money by text message. Why did it spread so widely?
options: Kenya's banks had branches in each village before 2007
Cell towers reached more people than banks
Kenya had more bank branches per person than any other country
Text messages were banned in most nearby countries at the time
Kenya had very few cell phones in use at the time

why.correct: The communications network already reached most Kenyans, while banks did not, so money services rode on the network that existed.
options: If banks had reached every village, M-Pesa would have filled little need; cell towers reached more people than banks did.
Right: the existing network made the service possible.
Bank branches were scarce, which is why phones mattered.
No such bans explain it.
It depended on wide cell phone use.

items.q: British cloth made in steam mills was sold cheaply in India in the 1800s. What was one effect on India?
options: India's hand weavers lost buyers and work
India soon built more steam mills than Britain had
India became the main supplier of steam engines to Britain
India stopped growing cotton
Indian weavers moved to Manchester to run its mills

why.correct: Cheap machine-made imports undercut hand weavers, so industry in one place could shrink work in another.
options: Right: cheap factory cloth undercut India's hand weaving, a cost of industrialization felt in a colony.
Britain led in mills in this period; India mainly supplied raw cotton.
Britain built the steam engines; India's hand weavers lost buyers to cheap mill cloth.
India kept growing cotton, much of it for British mills.
There was no large migration of weavers from India to run British mills.

items.q: In world-economy terms, why do countries often classed as core have a smaller share of workers in the primary sector than countries often classed as periphery?
options: Core countries have very few farms or mines left to work in
Machines do more farm work, and more jobs are in services
Periphery countries ban service jobs to protect farming
Primary-sector jobs pay more in the periphery than in the core
Periphery countries have fewer farms than core countries

why.correct: The core is defined by high-wage service, research and decision jobs and productive industry; farming there uses machines and few workers, so the primary share is small.
options: Core countries still farm and mine a lot; they just need fewer workers to do it.
Right: high productivity in farming frees workers for tertiary, quaternary and quinary jobs.
There is no such ban; many people farm because other jobs are scarce.
Pay is usually lower in the periphery; the difference is in the mix of jobs available.
Periphery countries often have more people in farming; machines and service jobs shrink the primary share in the core.

items.q: According to the chart, in which years did the secondary sector employ its largest share of Country B's workers?
options: 2020, at its highest point
1970 and 2020, at both ends of the chart

why.correct: The secondary line rises to 30% in 1990, holds at 30% in 2000, then falls.
options: The secondary line is lower then (15% and 24%).
Right: the secondary line peaks at 30% in both 1990 and 2000.
The secondary share had fallen by then, to 26% and 21%.
In 2020 the secondary share is 21%, below its 1990 and 2000 peak.
The secondary share is 15% in 1970 and 21% in 2020, below its 30% peak in 1990 and 2000.

items.q: Which statement best describes the change in Country B's economy from 1970 to 2020?
options: Services gave way to factories, then to farm work
Farm and mine work gave way to factories, then services
Factories replaced services as the largest sector by 2020
The primary sector grew while services shrank
The three sectors each stayed about the same size

why.correct: A describe answer gives the direction and the order of the change: primary down throughout, secondary up then down, tertiary up to 70% of workers.
options: The chart runs the other way: primary work fell, secondary rose then fell, and services grew.
Right: primary falls the whole time; secondary rises then falls; tertiary rises to 70%.
In 2020 services employ 70% and factories 21%.
Both lines move the other way: primary falls, services grow.
The primary line falls 51 points and the tertiary line rises 45; the mix shifted a great deal.

items.q: What best explains the steady fall of the primary line in Country B?
options: Machines let fewer farmers grow the food
Country B stopped growing food and now imports it instead
Farm prices rose so high that people stopped buying food
Primary workers were moved into the quinary sector by law
The country ran out of land suitable for farming in 1970

why.correct: As machines and new methods raise output per farmer, fewer farm jobs are needed, so workers shift into the secondary and tertiary sectors.
options: Right: higher farm output per worker frees people for factory and service work.
Fewer farmers does not mean no farming; machines raise output per worker.
Rising food prices would not cut farm jobs this way; machines let fewer farmers grow the food.
No law is needed: people move to better-paid town jobs as farms need fewer hands.
The fall is gradual over 50 years, which fits rising farm productivity, not a sudden loss of land.

items.q: A plant turns 10 tonnes of copper ore into 1 tonne of copper. Where does least cost theory predict the plant will locate?
options: Next to the market, because the product is heavier
Near the mine, because the product weighs far less than the ore
Halfway between the mine and the market
At the port closest to the buyers
In the largest city of the country

why.correct: Copper smelting is weight-losing: the ore weighs ten times the product. Least cost theory puts the plant near the raw material, so the heavy ore travels the least.
options: The product is lighter, not heavier: it weighs a tenth of the ore.
Right: shipping 1 tonne of copper costs less than shipping 10 tonnes of ore.
Halfway means hauling the heavy ore part of the way for nothing.
A port near the buyers would mean shipping the heavy ore the whole distance.
A city may be the market, but the theory weighs transport costs, which favor the mine.

items.q: Why should students compare the HDI values of two countries only within the same UNDP report?
options: The HDI measures income alone in newer reports
Each report revises values, even for back years
The HDI is published once in twenty years
Each report uses a different set of 3 countries
Older reports measured income alone

why.correct: Composite indices are revised with each report, and back years are recalculated, so only values from one edition are comparable.
options: The HDI combines health, education and income in every report; values are revised between reports.
Right: composite indices are recalculated each edition.
It is published far more often than that.
Each report covers nearly every country.
The HDI has combined health, education and income since it began.

items.q: Iceland passed a law in 2017 that requires larger employers to prove they pay women and men equally for work of equal value. What does this show?
options: Development by itself closes the gender wage gap
The gender wage gap exists in periphery countries alone
Policy, not income alone, shapes opportunity
Women in Iceland work in the informal sector
Iceland's wage gap closed as soon as it became wealthy

why.correct: A pay gap can persist in a rich country, so governments use policies such as Iceland's law to close it.
options: If development alone closed it, a rich country would not need such a law.
Iceland has a very high HDI, yet it acted on a pay gap.
Right: even a very high-income country used a law to push for equal pay.
The law is about formal employers' pay, not informal work.
Iceland passed a law in 2017 to enforce equal pay, which shows policy, not wealth alone, shapes opportunity.

items.q: In invented Country K, one worker can make 20 shirts or 4 phones in a day. In invented Country L, one worker can make 30 shirts or 10 phones. Which country has the comparative advantage in shirts?
options: Country L, because its workers make more shirts
Neither, because Country L makes more of both goods
Country K, because each shirt costs it fewer phones
Country L, because each shirt costs it fewer phones
Both equally, because each makes two goods

why.correct: Comparative advantage goes to the country that gives up less to make a good. A shirt costs Country K 4 / 20 = 0.2 phones and Country L 10 / 30, about 0.33 phones, so K has the comparative advantage in shirts.
options: Making more shirts is an absolute advantage; comparative advantage compares what each country gives up.
L has the absolute advantage in both, but each country still has a comparative advantage in one good.
Right: a shirt costs K 0.2 phones and L about 0.33 phones.
The costs are the other way: each shirt costs L about 0.33 phones and K only 0.2.
Making two goods does not make the costs equal: 0.2 and 0.33 phones a shirt differ.
